prompt: How does `load_raw.py` land the publishers' prices in the warehouse?

choices.text: As `jsonb`, one document per line
choices.why: Right. Staging parses it; raw keeps it untouched.

choices.text: Parsed into typed columns, with bad rows dropped on the way
choices.why: That would be cleaning in the raw layer, which the lesson keeps out of it.

choices.text: As CSV text files in the warehouse directory
choices.why: They go into a table, not a file.

choices.text: As one row per publisher with all its prices in an array
choices.why: Each price stays its own row, exactly as the API sent it.

prompt: Why does `load_raw.py` ask the shop for each table's columns instead of having them written in the script?
hint: What happens when the shop adds a column?

choices.text: PostgreSQL requires it for `COPY`
choices.why: `COPY` works with any matching table; the reason is change.

choices.text: A new column arrives without editing the loader
choices.why: Right. The decision about it is then made in staging.

choices.text: It hides the shop's schema from the warehouse's users
choices.why: The raw tables show the shop's schema exactly.

choices.text: It makes the copy faster
choices.why: The columns are read once per table; speed is unaffected.

prompt: Before cleaning, 839 of the 909 prices matched a book. How many did not?
Match each problem in the publishers' feed to the expression in `staging/prices.sql` that fixes it.
Why does the lesson refuse to replace a missing price with the average price of the publisher's books?

choices.text: Averages are slow to compute in SQL
choices.why: They are cheap; the objection is what the number would claim.

choices.text: It would invent a fact nobody said
choices.why: Right. Fix how a value is written, never what it is.

choices.text: The publisher would see it
choices.why: Nobody outside sees the warehouse; the problem is internal truth.

choices.text: Missing prices are illegal under the LGPD
choices.why: Prices are not personal data.

prompt: `raw.events` held 18,308 deliveries and `staging.events` 18,230 events. How many deliveries were second copies?
Two customers really bought the same book at the same second from the same shop. Which way of deduplicating would wrongly merge them?
hint: Which definition of the same ignores identity?

choices.text: By an id the producer assigned
choices.why: Two purchases get two ids, so they stay apart.

choices.text: By the order id
choices.why: Two purchases are two orders.

choices.text: `SELECT DISTINCT` on book and time
choices.why: Right. Equal columns are not the same event.

choices.text: A business key that includes the customer
choices.why: The customer tells them apart.

prompt: `staging/events.sql` numbers the copies of each event with the window function ___() and keeps copy number one.
hint: It numbers rows within a partition.

prompt: Joining completed orders to their payments and their lines gave a revenue of R$ 4,173,913.50 instead of R$ 2,121,622.90. Why?
hint: How many rows does an order with three lines become?

choices.text: Refunded orders were counted
choices.why: Both queries filter on completed orders.

choices.text: Each payment repeats once per line
choices.why: Right. That is fan-out.

choices.text: Payments include tax that lines do not
choices.why: Lines and payments agree to the cent, as the reconciliation showed.

choices.text: Each order appears in two shops
choices.why: An order belongs to one shop.

prompt: A query sums `orders.discount_cents` after joining orders to order lines. On which days will its total be right?

choices.text: Every day, because the join is on the key
choices.why: A join on the key still repeats the order once per line.

choices.text: No day, because discounts are on lines
choices.why: The question puts the discount on the order.

choices.text: When each one had one line
choices.why: Right. Which is why the bug hides until a busy day.

choices.text: Weekends only
choices.why: Busier days make it worse, not better.

prompt: Which of these protect a transformation against fan-out? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Counting rows before and after each join
choices.why: Yes. An unexpected change is the symptom.

choices.text: Summing columns only at the grain they live at
choices.why: Yes. Revenue from lines, not payments repeated by lines.

choices.text: Aggregating each side to a common grain before joining
choices.why: Yes. Then the join matches one row to one row.

choices.text: Adding `DISTINCT` to the sum
choices.why: `sum(DISTINCT amount)` merges two different orders that cost the same.

prompt: Why is `is_sale` derived in `staging/orders.sql` rather than written as `status = 'completed'` in each report?

choices.text: A boolean is smaller than text
choices.why: Size is not the argument.

choices.text: Reports cannot filter on text
choices.why: They can; the risk is filtering differently.

choices.text: So it is defined once
choices.why: Right. One definition of a sale, inherited by everything that reads it.

choices.text: The shop's status column will be removed
choices.why: Nothing says so; the reason is consistency.

prompt: On 6 and 7 March there were 623 orders. Dated in UTC, 34 of them fell on 8 March. How many orders did the UTC dating move from Friday the 6th to Saturday the 7th, if Friday had 279 in São Paulo and 252 in UTC?
A colleague runs the warehouse on a server set to UTC and writes `ordered_at::date` in a new report. Which orders end up on the wrong day?
hint: São Paulo is three hours behind UTC.

choices.text: None; `::date` uses the order's own zone
choices.why: A `timestamptz` keeps no zone; `::date` uses the session's.

choices.text: Every order, shifted by three hours
choices.why: Only the date changes, and only for some.

choices.text: Orders placed before 03:00 in São Paulo
choices.why: Those are already the next day in UTC and in São Paulo alike.

choices.text: Those after 21:00 local
choices.why: Right. In UTC they are already the next day.

prompt: Why can the joins in `marts/daily_sales.sql` not fan out?

choices.text: They go up, from each line to one order and one book
choices.why: Right. Each line matches exactly one row on the other side.

choices.text: They use `USING` instead of `ON`
choices.why: `USING` is shorthand; it does not change how many rows match.

choices.text: The mart has a primary key
choices.why: It has none, and a key would not stop a join multiplying rows.

choices.text: Staging removed duplicates
choices.why: Orders and lines had none; direction is the reason.

hint: Where does its order come from?

choices.text: It stops at the first file that fails
choices.why: That is a strength: nothing runs on top of a broken table.

choices.text: Its order comes from file names
choices.why: Right. Nothing records that one table needs another.

choices.text: It hides NOTICE messages
choices.why: That keeps the output readable; warnings and errors still show.

choices.text: It needs Python
choices.why: It is a shell script calling psql.

prompt: The mart, the lines and the payments all gave R$ 2,121,622.90. If the mart had been higher than the payments, what would that most likely mean?

choices.text: A till charged too little
choices.why: That would make lines and payments disagree, not the mart.

choices.text: The mart fanned out
choices.why: Right. A higher total after joins is the classic symptom.

choices.text: Some payments were refunded
choices.why: Every total is over completed orders only.

choices.text: The raw layer was loaded twice
choices.why: Then lines and payments would be doubled as well.

prompt: Order the layers and steps that build `marts.daily_sales`.
items: load_raw.py copies the shop into raw
staging derives order_date, is_sale and line_cents
the mart joins lines up to orders and books, and groups

prompt: A new mart reports views per book per day from `raw.events` directly, dating each event by the file it landed in. Which two errors does it carry?
hint: What did staging fix about events?

choices.text: Fan-out and a UTC date
choices.why: There is no join to fan out, and file dates are local.

choices.text: Missing prices and hyphenated ISBNs
choices.why: Those are the prices' problems, not the events'.

choices.text: Duplicates counted, and late events on the wrong day
choices.why: Right. Staging removes the copies and dates by event time.

choices.text: None, if the files are complete
choices.why: Complete files still carry duplicates and late arrivals.
